# Kuhn Poker {.unnumbered}

In the classroom experiment, the students played @sec-efg-kuhn-poker against an Open AI bot. First, we will describe behavioral strategies for players 1 and 2 that form a Nash equilibrium.


## All Nash equilibria

All Nash equilibria in behavioral strategies are given by the following
four tables. Kuhn's original paper derives the complete set of equilibria
[@kuhn1950poker]. A single equilibrium can also be computed by linear programming directly from the induced
normal form, with $2^6=64$ pure strategies per player
and a $64\times64$ payoff matrix, or from the sequence-form linear program, with $13$ sequences per player. The equilibrium
family is parameterized by the probability
$\alpha\in[0,1/3]$ that player 1 opens with a bet holding
$J$. Player 2's equilibrium strategy is unique. The additional parameter $\rho$ specifies player 1's probability of calling with $K$
after check–bet and it is defined as
$$
\rho=1 \quad\text{if }0\leq\alpha<\frac13,
\qquad
\rho\in[0,1] \quad\text{if }\alpha=\frac13.
$$

### Player 1: opening move

| Card | Check | Bet |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| $J$ | $1-\alpha$ | $\alpha$ |
| $Q$ | $1$ | $0$ |
| $K$ | $1-3\alpha$ | $3\alpha$ |

### Player 1: after check–bet

| Card | Fold | Call |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| $J$ | $1$ | $0$ |
| $Q$ | $\frac23-\alpha$ | $\frac13+\alpha$ |
| $K$ | $1-\rho$ | $\rho$ |

### Player 2: after an opening check

| Card | Check | Bet |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| $J$ | $\frac23$ | $\frac13$ |
| $Q$ | $1$ | $0$ |
| $K$ | $0$ | $1$ |

### Player 2: facing an opening bet

| Card | Fold | Call |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| $J$ | $1$ | $0$ |
| $Q$ | $\frac23$ | $\frac13$ |
| $K$ | $0$ | $1$ |



At $\alpha=1/3$, player 1 always opens with a bet holding $K$. The
information set after checking with $K$ and facing a bet is therefore
unreachable under that player's own strategy, regardless of player 2's
choices. Any value of $\rho$ gives the same distribution over terminal
histories against every strategy of player 2. The usual choice $\rho=1$
prescribes calling with the highest card even at this unreachable
information set.

At $\alpha=0$, player 1 always opens with a check. Player 2's responses to an
opening bet still have to be as specified above since they prevent profitable
unilateral deviations by player 1.

Every admissible pair $(\alpha,\rho)$ as defined above gives a Nash equilibrium and there
are no other equilibria. Since the game is zero-sum, all have the same
expected net payoff $v$ for player 1, which is the *value of the game*. The value is 

$$
v=-\frac1{18} \approx -0.056.
$$
in chips per hand. Hence Player 2 has a small advantage under equilibrium play.

## Classroom play against an equilibrium bot

$950$ completed hands were recorded from 3 to 10
November 2026.  Students played $475$
hands in the role of either player. The records contains $11$ browser profiles and $13$ nicknames. The bot used the fixed
equilibrium strategy with $\alpha=1/3$ and $\rho=1$. 

### Statistics

| Student's seat | Hands | Hands won | Net chips | Chips per hand | Equilibrium expectation per hand |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Player 1 | $475$ | $248$ | $-46$ | $-0.097$ | $-0.056$ |
| Player 2 | $475$ | $255$ | $+51$ | $+0.107$ | $+0.056$ |
| *All student hands* | **$950$** | **$503$** | **$+5$** | **$+0.005$** | **$0$** |

Students won $503/950\approx52.9\%$ of hands.
This result alone says nothing about whether the students used equilibrium strategies. At equilibrium, Player 2 expects to gain over $475$ hands $475/18\approx 26.39$ chips. The standard deviation of the $475$-hand total is $29.5$ chips.

### Decisions at observed information sets

The table counts a student's decision only when its information set was
reached. The equilibrium benchmark is the fixed strategy $\alpha=1/3$, $\rho=1$ used by
the bot when it occupies the same seat. 

| Student's seat and info set | Action |  Benchmark | Observed choices |
|:--|:--|:--:|:--:|
| Player 1 opens with $J$ | Bet | $1/3$ | $52/168$ ($31.0\%$) |
| Player 1 opens with $Q$ | Bet | $0$ | [$97/147$ ($66.0\%$)]{style="color: #b42318; font-weight: 700"} |
| Player 1 opens with $K$ | Bet | $1$ | $142/160$ ($88.8\%$) |
| Player 1 holds $J$ after check–bet | Call | $0$ | $5/54$ ($9.3\%$) |
| Player 1 holds $Q$ after check–bet | Call | $2/3$ | $19/34$ ($55.9\%$) |
| Player 1 holds $K$ after check–bet | Call | $1$ | $4/4$ ($100\%$) |
| Player 2 holds $J$ after an opening check | Bet | $1/3$ | $34/71$ ($47.9\%$) |
| Player 2 holds $Q$ after an opening check | Bet | $0$ | [$42/55$ ($76.4\%$)]{style="color: #b42318; font-weight: 700"} |
| Player 2 holds $K$ after an opening check | Bet | $1$ | $114/131$ ($87.0\%$) |
| Player 2 holds $J$ facing an opening bet | Call | $0$ | [$19/82$ ($23.2\%$)]{style="color: #b42318; font-weight: 700"} |
| Player 2 holds $Q$ facing an opening bet | Call | $1/3$ | [$70/98$ ($71.4\%$)]{style="color: #b42318; font-weight: 700"} |
| Player 2 holds $K$ facing an opening bet | Call | $1$ | $37/38$ ($97.4\%$) |

Red marks the largest departures from the fixed benchmark. Player 1's $Q$
bets and Player 2's $J$ calls reduce expected payoff against this bot. However, Player 2's $Q$ bets and  $Q$ calls do not, although they are different from the
equilibrium play. Player 1's $J$ and $K$ opening rates are roughly compatible
with another equilibrium parameter, $\alpha\approx0.30$. The counts pool
repeated decisions from recorded $11$ browser profiles.

### Which decisions reduced expected payoff?

Against this fixed bot, the largest summed conditional expected losses came
from Player 2 calling an opening bet with $J$ ($19$ calls; $19$ chips),
Player 1 opening with a bet holding $Q$ ($97$ bets; $16.17$ chips), and
Player 2 checking with $K$ after a check ($17$ checks; $6.80$ chips).
Across all $139$ costly choices ($13.3\%$ of $1{,}042$ student decisions),
the summed conditional expected loss was $49.97$ chips. This compares
decisions using only the student's card and public history; it does not
explain the realized $+5$-chip result.
